title: Commented-out activity logging and unused props in QuestionHeader
evidence: Props type defines `userId` and `articleId` (lines 19-20) that are never used. Lines 37-52 contain commented-out activity logging code that was removed during a refactor but not cleaned up. Line 23-25 defines a local `ActivityType` that is unused. The function `onButtonClick` is declared `async` but performs no async work.
impact: Dead code increases maintenance burden and misleads reviewers about intended functionality.
recommendation: Remove unused props, commented code, and unused type. Change `onButtonClick` to synchronous.

title: Extensive `any` types in MC question content
category: Same root cause as Reading Advantage
evidence: Line 27: `const [activeQuestion, setActiveQuestion] = useState(null) as any` — explicit `any` cast bypassing TypeScript. Line 28: `const [responses, setResponses] = useState<any[]>([])` — untyped response array. Line 51: `const shuffleArray = (array: any[])` — generic any array parameter.
impact: Loss of type safety for quiz response data. Errors in response shape won't be caught at compile time, increasing risk of runtime failures for primary students during quizzes.
recommendation: Define proper types for `activeQuestion` (string | null), `responses` (array of `{question: string, answer: string, isCorrect: string}`), and `shuffleArray` parameter.

title: Hardcoded question total of 5 in MC quiz
evidence:
`

{t("descriptionSuccess2", { score: correct ?? 0, total: 5 })}

` — hardcoded `total: 5` does not match actual question count. The quiz content component uses `questions.length` dynamically (line 176-177 of mc-question-content.tsx), but the completion card always shows "out of 5".
impact: If question count changes from 5, the completion score display will be incorrect, confusing primary students about their performance.
recommendation: Pass actual question count from `questionsData.questions.length` or use a constant.

title: Duplicate ActivityType import sources in MCQuestionCard
evidence: Line 3 imports `AnswerStatus, QuestionState` from `@/types/enum` (local types). Line 14 imports `activityType as ActivityType` from `@reading-advantage/db` (Drizzle package). Two different ActivityType sources exist in the same file — the local enum and the DB enum. The local one is used for `AnswerStatus` and `QuestionState`, but `ActivityType` comes from the DB package.
impact: If the DB enum and local enum diverge, quiz type routing could silently break. Mixed import sources confuse maintainers.
recommendation: Consolidate to a single ActivityType source (prefer the DB enum since it's the source of truth).

title: Missing error/loading handling in MC quiz finish submission
category: Same root cause as Reading Advantage
evidence: `handleFinishQuiz()` calls `finishQuiz()` server action with no error boundary or user-facing error state. On failure (line 143-146), only a generic toast `"Failed to finish quiz"` is shown with destructive styling — no retry mechanism, no error details logged, and the quiz state remains paused (`setPaused(true)` called at line 123) with no way to unpause.
impact: If the server action fails, the quiz is stuck in a paused state. Primary students have no way to retry or recover without navigating away and back.
recommendation: Reset paused state on error and provide a retry button in the error toast.

title: Unsafe type cast on question data in MCQuestionCard
category: Same root cause as Reading Advantage
evidence: `questions={questionsData.questions as MCQuestion[]}` — unsafe cast from the question response to `MCQuestion[]` type without runtime validation. No length check or shape validation before rendering.
impact: Runtime crash if server returns unexpected data shape. No error boundary catches this.
recommendation: Add Zod validation or minimum array length check before passing to child component.

title: Hardcoded English strings in MC quiz component
evidence: Lines 136-140: `"Quiz finished successfully"` hardcoded English toast. Lines 143-147: `"Failed to finish quiz"` hardcoded English toast. Lines 184-189: `"Feedback: "` hardcoded label. Lines 224-228 and 234-238: `"Please select an option to continue"` hardcoded English toast. All bypass the next-intl translation system.
impact: Non-English primary students see English messages during quiz interactions, breaking localization for young learners who may not read English.
recommendation: Replace all hardcoded strings with `t()` translation calls.

title: SA question card fetches data server-side with no authorization check
category: Same root cause as Reading Advantage
evidence: The server component calls `getQuestionsByArticleId(articleId, ActivityType.SA_QUESTION)` with the `articleId` prop passed directly from the parent. No `currentUser()` check, role verification, or ownership validation is performed. Any user who navigates to the article page can fetch quiz data.
impact: Unauthorized access to quiz content; data leakage across tenants if `articleId` is guessable.
recommendation: Add `currentUser()` call and verify the user has access to the article (e.g., enrolled in a class that assigned it, or the article is public).

title: Undefined `session` variable in `handleFinishQuiz` will throw ReferenceError
evidence: `update({ user: { ...session?.user } })` references `session` which is never declared in the component scope. Line 62 destructures only `user` from `useSession()`, not `session`. This will throw a `ReferenceError` at runtime when the user completes a short-answer quiz.
impact: Quiz completion flow crashes for every short-answer question; users cannot finish SA quizzes.
recommendation: Replace `session?.user` with the `user` variable from line 62, or destructure `session` from `useSession()`.

title: Typo `isPanding` instead of `isPending`
evidence: `const [isPanding, startTransition] = useTransition()` and references at lines 161 and 165 use `isPanding` instead of the conventional `isPending`. This is a variable naming typo; the code functions but is inconsistent with React conventions.
impact: Readability and maintainability; contributors may confuse `isPanding` with a typo for `isPending`.
recommendation: Rename `isPanding` to `isPending`.

title: Hardcoded `preferredLanguage: "en"` ignores multilingual context
evidence: The `getFeedback` call passes `preferredLanguage: "en"` as a hardcoded string. The app supports five locales (en, th, cn, tw, vi) via `next-intl`. Primary students using Thai, Chinese, or Vietnamese will receive AI feedback generated in English, which defeats the purpose of localized education.
impact: Non-English-speaking primary students get feedback in the wrong language, reducing learning effectiveness.
recommendation: Pass the current locale from `useLocale()` or the session as `preferredLanguage`.

title: Hardcoded Thai translation in sentence component ignores user locale
evidence: `{list.translation.th}` always renders the Thai translation regardless of the user's selected locale. The `Sentence` interface defines translations for th, cn, tw, and vi (lines 21-26), but only `.th` is used. Primary students using Chinese, Vietnamese, or English will see Thai text.
impact: Non-Thai-speaking primary students receive translations in the wrong language.
recommendation: Use `useLocale()` to select the appropriate translation key (`th`, `cn`, `tw`, `vi`, or fall back to a default).

title: Leftover `console.log(words)` in word-list component
evidence: `console.log(words)` is a debug statement left in production client-side code. This dumps the entire word list to the browser console on every render.
impact: Debug noise in production; potential information disclosure of vocabulary data in client console.
recommendation: Remove the `console.log(words)` statement.

title: Unused `loading` state variable in word-list and sentence components
evidence: `const [loading, setLoading] = useState<boolean>(false)` is declared and never set to `true`. The loading skeleton UI at line 108 (`{loading && words ? ...}`) will never render. Identical issue exists in `sentence.tsx:40`.
impact: Dead code; loading skeleton is unreachable. Misleads future developers into thinking loading state is managed.
recommendation: Either implement the loading state management or remove the unused variable and skeleton code path.

title: AudioButton polling interval at 5ms is excessively aggressive
category: Same root cause as Reading Advantage
evidence: `setInterval(() => { ... }, 5)` polls the audio element's `currentTime` every 5 milliseconds (200 checks/second). This is orders of magnitude more frequent than needed for playback position tracking.
impact: Unnecessary CPU usage; can cause battery drain on mobile devices (primary student tablets/phones); potential jank during audio playback.
recommendation: Increase interval to 250-500ms, which is sufficient for detecting playback position changes and still provides responsive stop behavior.

title: Email forgot-password template is a non-functional placeholder
evidence:
The template renders only `

Welcome, {firstName}!

`. This is not a password reset email; it is a generic welcome template. The forgot-password flow references this template but it does not contain reset instructions, a reset link, or any actionable content.
impact: Users requesting a password reset receive an unhelpful "Welcome" email instead of reset instructions.
recommendation: Replace with an actual password reset email template containing a reset link and instructions, or remove the dead template if the reset flow uses a different mechanism.

title: Student sign-in form bypasses auth adapter with direct fetch to `/api/auth/login`
category: Same root cause as Reading Advantage
evidence: `handleLogin()` calls `fetch("/api/auth/login", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ username: selectedStudentId, password: code }) })` directly. The teacher sign-in form (batch peer `teacher-signin-form.tsx:36,51`) uses `useAuth()` from `@reading-advantage/auth-client` with `login(email, password)`. This violates the adapter pattern: application code must call `auth.login()` not provider SDKs or direct HTTP.
impact: Inconsistent auth flows between student and teacher; student login bypasses any adapter-level audit logging, CSRF protection, or session management that the auth adapter provides.
recommendation: Migrate student sign-in to use the `useAuth()` adapter pattern, or document why the direct API call is intentional and ensure the `/api/auth/login` route applies equivalent protections.

title: Classroom code sent as plaintext password in student login request
evidence: The login body sends `{ username: selectedStudentId, password: code }` where `code` is the classroom enrollment code (not a real password). The classroom code is a short, shareable string (typically 4-8 characters). Using it as a "password" means the credential is weak, shareable by design, and transmitted in plaintext over the wire.
impact: Classroom codes can be intercepted, shared, or brute-forced; students authenticate with a shared secret rather than individual credentials.
recommendation: Use a proper authentication mechanism for primary students (e.g., magic link, PIN, or session-based classroom enrollment) rather than reusing classroom codes as passwords.

title: Teacher sign-in form has hardcoded English strings bypassing i18n
evidence: Multiple UI strings are hardcoded in English: "Welcome to Primary Advantage" (line 68), "Enter your email below to login to your account" (line 70), "Email" (line 78), "Password" (line 98), "Forgot your password?" (line 104), "Signing in..." / "Login" (line 125), "Or continue with" (line 129), "Login with Google" (line 143), "Don't have an account?" / "Sign up" (lines 147-148). The student sign-in form correctly uses `useTranslations("AuthPage.signin")` for all strings.
impact: Thai, Chinese, Vietnamese, and other non-English speaking teachers see English-only auth UI.
recommendation: Replace all hardcoded strings with `useTranslations()` calls matching the student form pattern.

title: Teacher sign-in exposes OAuth URL with API host on client side
category: Same root cause as Reading Advantage
evidence: `window.location.href = \`${process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL ?? "http://localhost:3001"}/auth/google\`` exposes the API server hostname in the client bundle. The fallback `http://localhost:3001` suggests a development default that may leak into production if the env var is unset.
impact: Infrastructure details exposed; if `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` is unset in production, users are redirected to localhost.
recommendation: Ensure `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL` is always set in production, or use a relative path / Next.js route handler to proxy the OAuth redirect.

title: Forgot-password form never sends a real password-reset email; API call is commented out and form unconditionally reports success
evidence: The `onSubmit` handler (lines 18-52) contains a `fetch("/api/send", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ email }) })` call that is **entirely commented out** (lines 27-33), and a `sendPasswordResetEmail(firebaseAuth, ...)` call that is also commented out (lines 41-51). After the comments, line 34 unconditionally calls `setIsEmailSent(true)` and line 35 calls `setIsLoading(false)`. The success branch on lines 95-101 then renders the green "The email has been sent!" confirmation screen regardless of whether any email was actually sent. The form is the entry point from `app/[locale]/auth/forgot-password/page.tsx` (confirmed via the RSC manifest lookup: forgot-password/page imports `UserResetPassForm` from this file).
impact: Critical security and trust bug. A primary-age student, parent, or teacher who submits a forgotten-password request receives a "we sent you an email" confirmation but no email is ever sent. They will assume the email is in their inbox and never know their account is locked out. Worse, the form silently swallows the comment-history of the codebase (this file looks like a half-migrated firebase → first-party-port fork), and a follow-up note `// sendPasswordResetEmail(firebaseAuth, email, ...)` (line 41) reveals the prior implementation used Firebase. The `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` migration history section explicitly says auth is being migrated toward the first-party adapter pattern, but this forgot-password flow was left as dead code with a fake success path.
recommendation: Replace the entire `onSubmit` body with a real call to the first-party `auth` adapter (`auth.requestPasswordReset(email)` per AGENTS.md "Auth Adapter" contract) or to `POST /api/auth/reset-password` (which already exists as a route stub — see `app/api/auth/reset-password/route.ts` per the inventory batch 013). Remove the firebase comment block (lines 41-51). Add Zod validation for `email` at the form boundary and rate-limit the endpoint server-side per the root AGENTS.md "Rate limiting for login endpoints" requirement. Until the real integration ships, the form should at minimum call `await fetch("/api/auth/reset-password", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ email }) })` and only call `setIsEmailSent(true)` after `response.ok` (mirroring the pattern in `change-username-form.tsx:50-67`).

title: Forgot-password form is hardcoded English; bypasses the `next-intl` translation system used by every other auth screen
evidence: The component imports nothing from `next-intl` (the import block on lines 3-9 only has `React`, `cn`, `Button`, `Icons`, `Label`, `Input`, `ShieldCheck`). All copy is hardcoded English: "Forgot your password?" (line 59), "Enter your email and we'll send you a link to reset your password." (line 62), "Send Forgot Password Email" (line 88), "The email has been sent!. Please check your email to reset your password." (lines 98-99). The sibling signup form `user-signup-form.tsx` (file 2 of this batch) uses `useTranslations` indirectly via react-hook-form and Zod, and the sibling signin forms `student-signin-form.tsx` / `teacher-signin-form.tsx` (per batch 027) follow the same pattern. This file is the only auth form in `components/auth/` that bypasses `next-intl`.
impact: Medium. A Thai, Chinese (cn/tw), or Vietnamese user (the `lib/utils.ts:85-93` `convertLocaleFull` list shows 5 supported locales) who lands on the forgot-password page sees English text even when their `next-intl` locale is selected. For a primary-student/parent audience where literacy may be uneven, switching between English form text and Thai/Chinese page chrome is jarring and reduces trust. This is the same anti-pattern flagged in batch 029 (LR-029-014, formatDate without locale) and batch 031 (LR-031-014, hardcoded footer text).
recommendation: Wrap the copy in `useTranslations("Auth.forgotPassword")` and add a `Auth.forgotPassword` namespace to each of the 5 message files (`messages/en.json`, `th.json`, `cn.json`, `tw.json`, `vi.json`). Replace lines 59, 62, 88, 98-99 with `t("title")`, `t("description")`, `t("submitButton")`, `t("successHeading")` respectively. While doing this, also fix the double punctuation on line 98 ("sent!.").

title: "Terms of Service" and "Privacy Policy" anchor tags are `<a href="#">` dead links; required-consent legal documents are unreachable
evidence: The signup form's terms block (lines 159-169) renders `Terms of Service` (line 161) and `Privacy Policy` (line 165). Both anchors use `href="#"` which navigates to the same page (or scrolls to top) and never opens the actual legal documents. The parent route `app/[locale]/auth/signup/page.tsx` exists (RSC manifest lookup confirmed it imports `SignUpForm`); the static privacy and terms pages exist at `app/[locale]/(index)/privacy-policy/page.tsx` (162 lines) and `app/[locale]/(index)/terms/page.tsx` (136 lines) per the batch 004 manifest. The form's terms-checkbox (lines 146-158) is gated on `accepted` (line 31) which controls button enablement (line 175) — so a user can be blocked from signing up unless they check a box whose adjacent legal links do nothing.
impact: High. For a primary-student onboarding flow, the requirement that the user accepts terms and conditions is a compliance prerequisite (COPPA, GDPR-K, school district data-handling policies). If a parent clicks "Accept terms" without ever reading the linked documents, the consent is uninformed. From a UX standpoint, the underlines on `href="#"` give the visual impression that the documents are reachable, but they are not. A parent who clicks through and tries to verify the policy will see the page scroll and assume they missed it.
recommendation: Replace the `<a href="#">` anchors with `<Link href="/privacy-policy">` and `<Link href="/terms">` from `next-intl`'s `@/i18n/navigation` (the same `Link` import used on line 10). Both target routes already exist with full content per the inventory. Open the documents in a new tab (`target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer"`) so the user does not lose the signup form context. Document the consent flow in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` under a new "Auth consent" section.

title: `loading` state is declared and read but `setLoading` is never called; "Creating account..." text is unreachable dead state
evidence: Line 30 declares `const [loading, setLoading] = useState<boolean>(false);`. The button label on line 177 reads `loading ? "Creating account..." : "Sign up"`. However, a search across the file confirms `setLoading` is never invoked: the only references are the declaration on line 30 and the read on line 177. The actual in-flight signal is `isPanding` from `useTransition` (line 29) which gates the button's `disabled={!accepted || isPanding}` (line 175). The `setIsPanding`-equivalent comes for free from React's transition machinery; the manual `loading` state is a dead branch copied from a pattern where the submit was a plain `async` function.
impact: Low. The button label is the only UI surface affected. Because `isPanding` is true during the server action's pending phase, the button is disabled and shows its default label ("Sign up"). The user sees no "Creating account..." text during the in-flight period, which is a minor UX gap on slow connections. The dead state also indicates the codebase was partially converted from a non-transition submit to a `useTransition` submit, and the cleanup was missed.
recommendation: Either (a) remove the unused `loading`/`setLoading` state on line 30 and simplify the button label on line 177 to `Sign up` (cleaner), or (b) keep both states and drive the label from `isPanding` (`isPanding ? "Creating account..." : "Sign up"`). Option (b) preserves the UX intent with minimal code change. Add a comment on line 30 noting that `setLoading` is reserved for any future non-transition submit paths.

title: Signup form has no parent/guardian consent field; primary-age accounts are created from the same form as teacher accounts
evidence: The form schema (line 20 imports `signUpSchema` from `@/lib/zod`) collects only `name`, `email`, `password`, `confirmPassword` (defaultValues on lines 39-42). There is no role selector visible in the form (lines 25-188), no date-of-birth field, no parent-email field, no consent checkbox other than the terms-and-conditions checkbox on lines 146-158. The SignUpForm component is reused by `app/[locale]/auth/signup/page.tsx` (RSC manifest lookup confirmed), and the sibling signin forms `student-signin-form.tsx` (202 lines) and `teacher-signin-form.tsx` (155 lines) exist as separate components — which means there are two different signin paths but only one signup path that does not differentiate role. Per the inventory, `app/api/auth/impersonate`, `login`, `logout`, `register`, `reset-password`, `session` routes all exist as 2-line stubs (batch 013) — so the register backend is mostly stub. Whatever the backend chooses for role, the UI does not capture it.
impact: Medium. Primary-student adaptation risk. A primary-age student (typically 5-12) can complete this form on their own device without any parent/guardian gate. Without a date-of-birth or parent-email field, there is no way for the server to enforce COPPA verifiable parental consent, GDPR-K parental consent, or school-district-specific consent at signup time. The terms checkbox (lines 146-158) is a single click that any child can perform. The fact that the form has separate `student-signin-form` and `teacher-signin-form` siblings but only one signup form suggests the role was meant to be captured at signup but is not.
recommendation: Add a `role` field to `signUpSchema` in `lib/zod.ts` (with values `"student" | "teacher" | "admin"`) and render a radio group or Select on the signup form before the password fields. For the `"student"` role, add a required `dateOfBirth` field and a required `parentEmail` field with a confirmation token flow. Document the consent fields in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` under "Auth consent". The current single-form signup should not be live-shipped to a primary-student audience until role + consent capture is added.

title: Error handler in `onSubmit` is empty (all code commented out); failed username updates silently swallow the error and provide no user feedback
evidence: The catch block (lines 69-77) is structured as `catch (error) { /* toast({ title: "An error occurred.", description: "Please try again later.", variant: "destructive", }) */ } finally { setIsLoading(false); }`. The toast call (lines 70-74) is entirely commented out. The `finally` block on line 75-77 re-enables the submit button (`setIsLoading(false)`). There is no `console.error(error)` either, so the actual failure cause is lost. The success path on line 65-67 renders a `toast("Username updated.", { description: ... })` from `sonner`, so the toast wiring is in place — it just is not invoked on failure.
impact: High. A school admin (the most likely user of this form per its placement in `app/[locale]/(student)/settings/user-profile/page.tsx`) who tries to update their username and hits a network error or server-side validation failure sees the button re-enable, no toast, and no message. They will assume the update succeeded or, more likely, refresh the page and see the old username, then try again. With no feedback, multiple retries can hit rate limits and create audit noise. The AGENTS.md "Audit Logs" section requires logging for security-sensitive events; a silent-failure username change is not logged at the client either.
recommendation: Replace lines 69-77 with `catch (error) { console.error("Username update failed:", error); toast.error("Failed to update username. Please try again."); } finally { setIsLoading(false); }`. Use the destructive toast variant pattern that already exists in `sonner` (success on line 65 uses `toast(...)`, error counterpart is `toast.error(...)`). Add a server-side audit log entry per the AGENTS.md "Audit Logs" requirement. Consider parsing the response body to surface server-provided error reasons (`await response.json().then(b => b.message ?? "Failed")`) so the user sees the actual server message.

title: `useSession` from `@reading-advantage/auth-client` is imported but never used in the component
evidence: Line 20 imports `useSession` from `@reading-advantage/auth-client`. A scope-confined grep shows exactly one reference to `useSession` in the file — the import on line 20. The component uses `useRouter` (line 21), `useTranslations` (line 22), `useForm`, `zodResolver`, `useState`, `toast`, `Icons`, `Button`, `Form`, `FormControl`, `FormDescription`, `FormField`, `FormItem`, `FormLabel`, `FormMessage`, `Input` — but no `useSession`. The `userId` prop on line 34 is passed in from the parent page rather than read from the session client.
impact: Low. Bundle-size waste: importing `@reading-advantage/auth-client` pulls its tree-shake graph into the auth/settings bundle. Maintenance trap: a future reader assumes `useSession` is the source of `userId` and would search for its usage. The pattern is repeated across other settings forms (per the same anti-pattern flagged in earlier batches for unused imports).
recommendation: Remove line 20. If a future change needs the session client, add the import back at that time. The `userId` prop pattern on line 34 (parent-passed user id) is the correct approach for settings forms where the parent route already has the user context from the server.

title: Username field only validates `min(5)`; no allowlist, no profanity filter, no impersonation check for primary-student accounts
evidence: The inline Zod schema on lines 24-28 is `z.object({ name: z.string().min(5, { message: "Username must be at least 5 characters." }) })`. There is no `max(...)`, no `regex(...)` for allowed characters, no profanity/profanity-list filter, no check that the new username does not collide with an admin or teacher name (so a student could rename themselves to "Mr Johnson" or "Principal"). The submit path on line 50 sends `JSON.stringify(data)` to `PATCH /api/users/${userId}` — what the server validates is not visible in this file. For primary-age accounts, the username is likely displayed in the teacher dashboard and on the leaderboard (`components/leaderboard.tsx`), so a misleading username has classroom-visible impact.
impact: Medium. A primary-age student can rename themselves to impersonate a teacher, principal, or another student; can use a name with profanity or PII (e.g., a home address); can use unicode that renders inconsistently across devices. The form's only check is the 5-character minimum, which is purely a UX floor (preventing empty/very short names), not a safety check. The same root-cause pattern was flagged in batch 022 for `article-creation.tsx` and batch 023 for `classrooms-table.tsx` form-state drift.
recommendation: Extend the schema with a `regex(/^[a-zA-Z0-9_]{3,20}$/)` allowlist and `max(20)` ceiling, and add a profanity check (the `lib/permissions.ts` file per batch 079 might host a shared helper). The PATCH endpoint at `app/api/users/[id]/route.ts` (per batch 019, 116 lines) should mirror this with a server-side Zod schema and a uniqueness check. Document the username policy in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` under a new "User identity" section.

title: Tailwind typo `captoliza` (line 126) — class does not exist; intended `capitalize` styling is silently no-op
evidence:
Line 126 renders `
{row.getValue("title")}
`. The Tailwind v4 class `capitalize` is the correct utility (per `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` "Tailwind CSS v4"). The string `captoliza` does not match any Tailwind utility, so the class is dropped during purging and the title text is rendered in its raw case. A typo from copy-paste of similar text-transform utilities (`uppercase`, `lowercase`, `normal-case`, `capitalize`).
impact: Low. The article title's first-letter capitalization is silently broken. For English titles the visual difference is minor; for Thai / Chinese titles the difference is invisible (no word boundaries); for Vietnamese titles with diacritics the title is rendered exactly as stored.
recommendation: Replace `captoliza` with `capitalize` on line 126. Add a Tailwind ESLint plugin (`eslint-plugin-tailwindcss`) to the project's lint config to catch class typos at lint time. The same typo pattern was flagged in batch 027 (LR-027-N) for the sentence component.

title: Status map has no fallback; unknown statuses from the API render as empty cells with no UI signal
evidence: The status column (lines 157-175) defines a `map` with five keys: `READ`, `COMPLETED_MCQ`, `COMPLETED_SAQ`, `COMPLETED_LAQ`, `UNRATED` (lines 162-168). The render expression on line 171 is `map[status as keyof typeof map]`. If the API returns any other status string (e.g., a future `IN_PROGRESS`, `BOOKMARKED`, or a legacy status like `ASSIGNED` that was renamed in the Drizzle migration per apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md), `map[status]` returns `undefined` and React renders nothing. There is no fallback (`map[status] ?? status`), no `default:` branch, and no warning log. The status cell in the student's history table would appear blank.
impact: Medium. After a schema migration (Drizzle Phase 8 of `primary_advantage_drizzle_migration_20260526` per AGENTS.md) renames or adds an enum value, the history table silently loses the badge for affected rows. For a primary-student whose parent checks progress, an empty status cell looks like a data loss bug. The student model (`server/models/studentModel.ts`, 669 lines, batch 095) defines an `activityType` enum per AGENTS.md "Schema layout", so enum drift is a known risk.
recommendation: Add a fallback on line 171: `map[status as keyof typeof map] ?? status ?? "—"`. Even better, replace the lookup with a shared `getStatusLabel(status)` helper that lives in `lib/zod.ts` or `lib/utils.ts` (Zod enum + label map) and is reused by `reminder-reread-table.tsx` (batch 029) and `article-content.tsx` (batch 025). Document the status enum contract in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` under a new "Status values" section.

title: `parseInt(row.getValue("rated"))` produces `NaN` for non-numeric ratings and renders literal "NaN" in the table cell
evidence:
The `rated` column cell (lines 150-156) calls `parseInt(row.getValue("rated"))` (line 153) and renders the result inside `
{amount}
` (line 154). If the `rated` value is `null`, `undefined`, an empty string, a non-numeric string (e.g., `"N/A"`), or a float with units (e.g., `"4.5/5"`), `parseInt` returns `NaN`. React renders `NaN` as the literal text "NaN" in the cell. There is no `Number.isFinite(amount) ? amount : "—"` guard.
impact: Medium. After a database migration or a partial data import where some rows have null ratings, the table shows "NaN" in the rating cell for those rows. For a primary-student-facing history view, "NaN" is meaningless and looks like a rendering bug. The same pattern was flagged in batch 026 for `article-showcase-card.tsx` and batch 028 sibling — see `class-activity-chart.tsx` finding LR-028-012.
recommendation: Replace line 153 with `const raw = row.getValue("rated"); const amount = typeof raw === "number" ? raw : parseInt(String(raw), 10); const display = Number.isFinite(amount) ? amount : "—";` and render `{display}` on line 154. Even better, type the `ArticleRecord.rated` field as `number | null` (line 38) instead of `string` to avoid the parse entirely and use `Number.isFinite(rated) ? rated : "—"` at the cell.

title: All dashboard chart data is hardcoded; admins see fabricated activity metrics regardless of school or data state
evidence: Lines 27-35 declare `const weeklyActivityData` as a literal array of seven day records with hardcoded numbers (e.g., `students: 45, teachers: 8, articles: 23, questions: 156` for Monday). Lines 38-44 declare `const engagementData` as a literal array of five metrics. There is no `fetch(...)` call, no SWR / React Query hook, no props passed from a parent. The three exported components `WeeklyActivityChart` (line 65), `ClassEngagementChart` (line 118), and `ActivityMetricsChart` (line 154) all render directly from these hardcoded arrays. `ActivitySummaryCards` (line 213) computes totals from the same arrays and renders trend deltas like `"+12% from last week"` (line 242), `"+8% from last week"` (line 260), `"+15% from last week"` (line 280), `"-3% from last week"` (line 298) — none of which are computed. title: `parseInt(row.getValue("rated"))` produces `NaN` for missing/non-numeric ratings and renders literal "NaN" in primary-student history table

title: `fetchData` bypasses the shared data layer; every dashboard widget re-implements its own fetch with no caching, no SWR/React Query, no error toast
evidence: Lines 57-72 define `fetchData` as `const fetchData = React.useCallback(async () => { ... const response = await fetch(`/api/users/${user.id}/reminder-reread`); ... }`. The sibling file `article-records-table.tsx` (per batch 028) uses `useReactTable` with no fetch layer; the broader pattern is "each dashboard widget does its own `useEffect + fetch`".
impact: Medium. Without a shared data layer: (a) every widget has to re-implement caching, deduplication, and error UX; (b) network errors are silent (only `console.error`); (c) there is no request-level revalidation, so a write elsewhere won't refresh this view; (d) the `QueryClient` / SWR DevTools can't inspect dashboard traffic. title: `lastedLevel` variable in `formatDataForDays` is initialized once and never updated; chart always resets xpEarned to 0 each day, breaking the cumulative-XP narrative
evidence: Line 76 declares `let lastedLevel = 0;` outside the for-loop. Line 90 reads it as `let xpEarned = lastedLevel;`. The intent expressed in the comment on lines 88-89 ("get the latest level of the user for that day ... if level is dosent change then the user didnt complete any article that day return the last user updatedLevel") is clearly to carry the previous day's cumulative XP forward if no completion happened on the current day. However, `lastedLevel` is never reassigned inside the loop — only `xpEarned` is. The variable name itself is also a typo ("lasted" should be "latest"). The practical effect: at the start of every day, `xpEarned` is reset to 0 and only the day's own XP contributions are summed, producing a sawtooth chart that drops back to 0 each morning instead of a monotonically increasing cumulative XP line.

The narrative of "I earned 150 XP over the past week" requires the line to start at zero on day 1 and rise to the cumulative total. For a primary-student who checks their dashboard daily, the chart makes it look like they "lose" XP every night. The TypeScript type is implicitly `number` so the bug is silent — no compile error, no runtime error, just wrong math.
recommendation: Either (a) make the chart non-cumulative (rename to "Daily XP" and accept the sawtooth) — this would be the smaller change and arguably matches a more useful primary-student narrative ("how much XP did I earn today vs yesterday"), or (b) make the chart cumulative by tracking `xpEarned += delta` across days and assigning `lastedLevel = xpEarned` after each day's loop iteration. Fix the variable name typo: rename `lastedLevel` → `previousDayXp` (or `runningTotal`). Update the comment block on lines 88-89 to read clearly. Add a unit test that asserts the first day's value is 0 and the last day's value equals the sum of all `xpEarned` across the input.

title: Chart stroke references `var(--color-xp)` but `chartConfig.xp.color` is `var(--primary)`; the auto-generated CSS variable is undefined so the line may render with the fallback or be invisible
evidence: Line 122-126 declares `const chartConfig = { xp: { color: "var(--primary)" } } satisfies ChartConfig`. Line 309 renders `<Line stroke="var(--color-xp)" ... />`. The interaction with `useTheme` from `next-themes` (imported on line 25 but never destructured — see LR-029-007) suggests the chart was meant to adapt to theme, but the unresolved CSS variable breaks both light and dark themes.

title: Heatmap day-boundary uses UTC ISO date string; primary-student reading activity at 23:30 local time is bucketed into the wrong day for any non-UTC user
evidence: Lines 17-19 compute `const date = new Date(activity.createdAt); const dateString = date.toISOString().split("T")[0];`. `Date.prototype.toISOString()` always serializes in UTC (`YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ`). For a user in `Asia/Bangkok` (UTC+7) whose `createdAt` is `2026-06-26T23:30:00+07:00`, the ISO string is `2026-06-26T16:30:00.000Z`, and the `split("T")[0]` produces `"2026-06-26"` — which happens to match the local date. But for an activity logged at `2026-06-27T00:30:00+07:00` (30 minutes past midnight local time), the ISO string is `2026-06-26T17:30:00.000Z`, and the date bucket is `"2026-06-26"` — which is the PREVIOUS day from the user's perspective. The heatmap rolls activities that happen in the early-morning local hours into the previous calendar day, producing an off-by-one visualization. The same bug affects any user east or west of UTC, including the five supported locales (`en`, `th`, `cn`, `tw`, `vi` per `lib/utils.ts:85-93`).
impact: High. The heatmap is the canonical year-at-a-glance view of a primary-student's reading activity. Off-by-one bucketing means: (a) a student who reads every morning before school sees their pattern shifted by one day; (b) a parent reviewing the heatmap with their child sees activity on the wrong day; (c) for a teacher using the heatmap to identify engagement patterns, the shift can mislead interventions. The bug is silent — no error, no UI signal — so the misalignment is invisible to the user. The `createdAt` field is presumably a server-generated UTC timestamp (per Drizzle default conventions), so the fix is to bucket on local date components (`getFullYear/getMonth/getDate` in the user's timezone) rather than on the UTC ISO prefix.
recommendation: Replace lines 17-19 with:

title: `levels.indexOf(currentLevel)` returns `-1` for unknown CEFR levels; gauge displays a negative value and translation lookup throws at runtime
evidence:
Line 53 computes `value={(levels.indexOf(currentLevel) / levels.length) * 100}`. If `currentLevel` is not present in the hardcoded `levels` array (lines 24-44, 19 entries: `A0-`, `A0`, `A0+`, `A1-`, `A1`, ..., `C1+`, `C2`), `levels.indexOf(currentLevel)` returns `-1`, and the gauge value is approximately `-5.26` (-100/19). {td(currentLevel)}

The hardcoded array is missing any safety for the unknown-value case.
recommendation: Replace line 53 with:

Per `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` "Schema layout", the primary-advantage-specific tables and enums live in `packages/db/src/schema/primary.ts`. The `cefrLevel` (or similarly named) enum is the natural single-source-of-truth for the gauge levels, but it is not imported here — the UI ships its own copy. After any backend migration that adds a new level (e.g., `A0--` or `C2+`), the gauge and the translation lookup drift.
impact: Medium. Drift between the UI's hardcoded array and the backend enum is a known class of bug (cf. LR-029-003 for the status enum). For a primary-student dashboard, the level drives the gauge color and the description text; any new level added to the backend will appear in the database but not in the UI, triggering LR-029-015 (the unknown-level crash).
recommendation: Add a `cefrLevel` enum to `packages/db/src/schema/primary.ts` (paralleling the `activityType`, `flashcardType`, `cardState` enums listed in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md`). Re-export from `packages/db/src/schema/index.ts`. Import in this file: `import { cefrLevel } from "@reading-advantage/db"; const levels = Object.values(cefrLevel);`. The ordering of `Object.values` matches insertion order in TypeScript enums, so the gauge ordering is preserved. Document the enum-to-UI mapping contract in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` under a new "CEFR levels" section.

title: Non-standard CEFR sub-levels (`A0-`, `A0+`, `A1-`, ..., `C1+`) are intentional product divergence; the rationale is undocumented
category: Intentional product divergence that needs documentation
evidence: Lines 24-44 include the levels `A0-`, `A0`, `A0+`, `A1-`, `A1`, `A1+`, `A2-`, `A2`, `A2+`, `B1-`, `B1`, `B1+`, `B2-`, `B2`, `B2+`, `C1-`, `C1`, `C1+`, `C2`. The standard CEFR scale (per the Council of Europe's Common European Framework of Reference for Languages) has six levels: `A1`, `A2`, `B1`, `B2`, `C1`, `C2`. Adding sub-levels with `+/-` suffixes is a primary-student-appropriate adaptation (more granular progress signals for younger learners), but the divergence from the standard is not documented in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` or anywhere in the repository.
impact: Low. The non-standard levels themselves are not a bug — finer granularity is appropriate for primary students. The risk is for downstream consumers (the CEFR level may be shared with external systems like a school LMS or a parent-facing report) that expect the standard scale. Without documentation, future developers will not know which scale to use.
recommendation: Add a "CEFR scale" section to `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` documenting: (a) the full level list used in primary-advantage; (b) the rationale for sub-levels (finer-grained progress signals for primary students); (c) the mapping to standard CEFR (e.g., `A0-` and `A0` collapse to "pre-A1" in external reporting); (d) where the level is stored (Drizzle schema column) and where it is computed (presumably the level-setter component `student-cefr-level-setter.tsx` per batch 062).

title: `useTranslations` typed as `string | any`; type annotation lies about the return type and bypasses TypeScript safety
evidence: Line 22 declares `const td: string | any = useTranslations("Reports.level.description");`. `useTranslations` from `next-intl` returns the `TFunction` (a function reference with metadata), not `string`. The `string | any` annotation is a manually-written type that is incorrect and defeats the purpose of TypeScript. The same anti-pattern recurs in `user-recent-activity.tsx:30` (`const td: string | any = useTranslations("Reports.activityType");`) — see LR-029-036. The result: any caller of `td(...)` gets a type of `any`, so passing a wrong-typed argument (e.g., a number instead of a string key) is not caught at compile time. This is the precise scenario that triggered LR-029-015 (the unknown-level runtime crash).
impact: Low individually, but it is the root cause of why LR-029-015's runtime crash is not caught at compile time. Two files have the same pattern; future copies will too unless the type is corrected.
recommendation: Replace lines 22 and the parallel line 30 in `user-recent-activity.tsx` with the correct type: `const td = useTranslations("Reports.level.description");` (no annotation, let TypeScript infer `TFunction`). The `useTranslations` return type provides auto-completion and type-checking of the key argument. Add a CI lint rule to forbid `: string | any` annotations on `useTranslations` results. Pair this fix with the safe `td(currentLevel)` call from LR-029-015 to fully eliminate the runtime crash.

title: Hardcoded colon `:` separator in "Your level : A1" line breaks RTL locales and locale-specific punctuation
evidence:
Line 80 renders `
{t("yourlevel")} : {currentLevel}
`. The colon `:` is a hardcoded English punctuation. For `next-intl` locales that use different separators (Arabic `:` looks the same but the surrounding text direction may flip the natural reading order; CJK locales typically use `：` instead of `:`), the hardcoded colon produces inconsistent UI.
impact: Low. Five supported locales include `en`, `th`, `cn`, `tw`, `vi` (per `lib/utils.ts:85-93`); none of those are RTL, so the impact today is limited to the colon-glyph difference. The risk is for future locales added to the platform.
recommendation: Move the separator into the translation: `t("yourlevelWithSeparator", { level: currentLevel })` and add `"yourlevelWithSeparator": "Your level : {level}"` (en) / `"ระดับของคุณ : {level}"` (th) / `"您的级别 : {level}"` (cn) / etc. Or use a non-punctuated version: `t("yourlevel", { level: currentLevel })` with message `"Your level {level}"` (English reads OK; Thai/Chinese/Vietnamese readers typically prefer no separator at all). Document the i18n punctuation policy in `apps/primary-advantage/AGENTS.md` under a new "Punctuation" section.

title: Server component passes function prop onClick to Button, violating RSC serialization boundary
evidence: `FlashcardDashboard` is an `async` function component (making it a React Server Component). Line 82 passes `onClick={() => window.location.reload()}` as a prop to `<Button>`. The `Button` component (`components/ui/button.tsx`) does not use `"use client"`. In the RSC model, function props cannot cross the server-client boundary and React will throw a serialization error at runtime.

recommendation: Move the interactive portion into a client component wrapper, or use `"use client"` on the enclosing component/file that renders `<Button onClick={...}>`. Alternatively, use `form` action or `<Link>` for navigation-level reload.

title: Undefined `update`/`session` causes runtime ReferenceError on flashcard completion

The batch review calls on lines 93-100 may still succeed, but the session update silently fails, and the error is caught by the try/catch which shows a "Failed to save ratings" toast even though the ratings were likely saved.
recommendation: Remove lines 106-110 (the `update(...)` call) or replace with the correct auth-client API if session refresh is needed after card review.

title: Unused constant `AVAILABLE_LANGUAGES` and unused import `Languages`
