title: Suspicious gradient class `from-gray-gray-300` on the chat messages container; Tailwind will silently fail to apply the gradient
evidence: Line 174 reads `<div className="from-gray-gray-300 overflow-hidden rounded-xl border border-gray-200 bg-gradient-to-b to-white ...">`. The class `from-gray-gray-300` is invalid Tailwind: the gradient color stop syntax is `from-{color}-{shade}`, and `gray-gray-300` is not a valid shade. Tailwind v4 (per the package.json reference in the system reminder) will not generate a utility for this class, and the gradient will silently render as just `to-white` (a flat white-to-transparent fade). The intended class was likely `from-gray-300` (single `gray-300` shade). This is a typo from a copy-paste of a `from-{other}-gray-300` pattern.
impact: Low. Visual regression: the chat background does not have the intended gray-to-white vertical gradient. The chat messages area looks flatter than designed. For a primary-student UX, the design polish matters for engagement.
recommendation: Change line 174 to `from-gray-300` (single `gray` prefix). Verify the visual against the design spec or Figma source. This is a one-character fix and should be tracked under a `primary_advantage_css_typos_<date>` chore track.

title: Chatbot fetch uses relative URL `/api/assistant/lesson-chatbot` directly; no internal AI adapter layer per AGENTS.md
category: Intentional product divergence that needs documentation
evidence: Lines 47 and 95 both call `fetch("/api/assistant/lesson-chatbot", { method: "POST", body: ... })`. Per the root AGENTS.md "AI" section: "AI access must go through an internal adapter. Application code should call `ai.generateText()`, `ai.streamText()`, `ai.generateObject()`, `ai.embed()`. Internally, the adapter may use Vercel AI SDK, OpenAI SDK, Anthropic SDK, Google SDK, or local model runtimes. Application code must not depend directly on provider SDKs." This component depends on a relative Next.js API route, which is **not** an internal adapter call. The `/api/assistant/lesson-chatbot` route presumably uses Vercel AI SDK or OpenAI SDK internally (per the AGENTS.md "AI" section's "Vercel AI SDK may be used behind the adapter" rule), but the client bypasses any shared `ai.chat()` wrapper.
impact: Medium. Fork-specific divergence: the Primary Advantage app appears to have its own chatbot API route rather than reusing a shared `ai.chat()` adapter from `@reading-advantage/ai` (or whichever shared AI package exists). This is an "intentional product divergence that needs documentation" because the chatbot is a primary-student-specific feature, but the divergence is not documented in the component or the route handler. The blast radius is limited to lesson chatbot functionality, but it sets a pattern that other AI features (workbook generation, vocabulary generation, etc.) may also be bypassing shared adapters.
recommendation: Either (a) add a shared `ai.chat({ article, messages, options })` adapter to the `@reading-advantage/ai` package (or create the package if it does not exist), then have this component call `ai.chat(...)` instead of `fetch("/api/assistant/lesson-chatbot", ...)`; or (b) document the intentional divergence in the component's JSDoc and a top-of-file comment, citing the primary-student adaptation (e.g., "this lesson chatbot is intentionally a separate Next.js route because it requires a primary-student-specific system prompt that differs from the Reading Advantage upstream's general-purpose chatbot"). Track under a `primary_advantage_ai_adapter_integration_<date>` track that audits all `fetch("/api/assistant/...")` calls across `apps/primary-advantage`.

title: `<AvatarImage src={"" }>` with literal empty string; relies on `<AvatarFallback>` to render the initial
evidence: Line 224 reads `<AvatarImage src={"" } alt={user?.name || "User"} referrerPolicy="no-referrer" />`. The `src=""` literal is a known accessibility/perf anti-pattern: when `src` is an empty string, the browser sends a request to the current page URL as if it were an image source, producing a 404 or HTML response logged as an image error in the browser console. The `<AvatarFallback>` on lines 228-230 correctly renders the user's initial, so the empty `src` is just a placeholder waiting for a real user image URL. The implementation pattern should either omit the `<AvatarImage>` entirely when no URL is available, or compute `src={user?.image || undefined}` so the Avatar component skips the image request.
impact: Low. Each user message renders an `` request to the current page URL (logged as a 404 in DevTools). For a chatbot that the student uses heavily, the noise accumulates. There is no functional impact because the `` renders correctly.
recommendation: Replace `<AvatarImage src={""} alt={...} ...>` with `{user?.image ? <AvatarImage src={user.image} alt={...} ... /> : null}` or `src={user?.image || undefined}`. The `referrerPolicy="no-referrer"` is good and should be preserved. Track under a `primary_advantage_avatar_src_cleanup_<date>` chore.

title: Initial-load progress math uses `Math.ceil(progress / (100/14))`; for tasks 4 and 13 the rounding step restores a task ahead of the user's actual position
evidence: Lines 101-104 compute `taskWidth = 100 / 14; const taskNumber = Math.ceil(data.userLessonProgress.progress / taskWidth);`. The server-side progress value is written on lines 211 and 310 as `Math.round((newTask / 14) * 100)`. The two rounding steps disagree at certain tasks because the forward write rounds `N/14*100` to an integer, then the read divides back. Worked examples:
impact: Medium. On reload after task 4 or task 13 the user is silently moved one phase ahead. The DB now stores a `progress` value inconsistent with the `currentTask` index actually displayed. For a primary-student app, the lesson-summary step also marks the lesson as "completed" in some downstream consumers (the `setPaused(true)` branch on lines 111-113 and 301-303 plus the `progress >= 100` threshold elsewhere), so the off-by-one on task 13 could prematurely close the lesson, prevent the language-questions chatbot from ever being reached, and leave the user with no record of completing the chatbot.
recommendation: Pick one rounding strategy and use it on both sides. The cleanest fix is to compute `progress = Math.ceil((N / 14) * 100)` on write (line 211 and 310) and drop the `Math.ceil` on read (replace line 102-104 with `const taskNumber = Math.round(data.userLessonProgress.progress / taskWidth);` or simpler: skip the read math entirely and have the server return `currentTask` directly). Track under a `primary_advantage_lesson_progress_round_trip_<date>` follow-up track alongside the broader `assignmentController` audit (this batch is one of several that use the same `(N/14)*100` encoding).

title: `progress` percentage on the sidebar uses floating-point division then rounded-to-integer width, producing a wrong width for several tasks
evidence: Line 712 reads `style={{ width: `${(currentTask / 14) * 100}%` }}`. For `currentTask=4`, `4/14*100 = 28.571…%`; the CSS `width: 28.571%` is rounded by the browser to 1 fractional pixel which differs from the server-side `Math.round(4/14*100) = 29%` (line 211, line 310). The displayed bar therefore lags the stored progress by ~0.4 percentage points on task 4, ~0.7 points on task 13, and 0 elsewhere. The sidebar progress text on line 693-697 also shows the integer `currentTask`, so the bar visibly disagrees with the text by a hairline amount on tasks 4 and 13.
impact: Low. Visual only; the bug is invisible to most users and only shows up as a ~1px misalignment between the numeric "Task N of 14" label and the white progress bar fill. For a primary-student UX this is a polish regression, not a functional one.
recommendation: Match the bar width to the value the server stores: `style={{ width: `${Math.round((currentTask / 14) * 100)}%` }}` on line 712. Or, even better, expose the server's stored `progress` field through `getAssignmentById` and render `width={progress}%` so the bar always matches the persisted state. Track under a `primary_advantage_progress_bar_width_rounding_<date>` chore.

title: `TaskIntroduction` is rendered with `onCompleteChange={() => {}}`; the task tries to notify the parent of completion but the orchestrator discards it
evidence: Lines 385-389 render `<TaskIntroduction article={...} onCompleteChange={() => {}} />`. Per `apps/primary-advantage/components/lesson/task/task-introduction.tsx:30-43`, `TaskIntroduction` declares `interface TaskIntroductionProps { article: Article; onCompleteChange: (complete: boolean) => void; }` and the body calls `onCompleteChange(true)` inside a `useEffect(..., [onCompleteChange])` on lines 41-43. The orchestrator passes a no-op, so the notification is silently dropped. The same is true for the other task components rendered with a no-op completion hook in `getTaskComponent` (only `TaskIntroduction` declares the prop, but the surrounding pattern is consistent: the orchestrator does not track per-task completion).
impact: Medium. The lesson-progress bar has no completion gate. The "Next Task" button is always enabled (lines 651), so a primary student can skip directly from the introduction to the next phase without reading the lesson goals or article summary. This is a primary-student adaptation risk: the introduction is the recommended pre-reading step and skipping it short-circuits the motivation loop. Other task components do not declare `onCompleteChange`, so they never had this hook — but the lesson-progress bar also lacks the parallel `phaseCompletion` array it once had (lines 149-161 are commented-out). The fork appears to have removed the per-phase gating but kept the dead prop interface on `TaskIntroduction`.
recommendation: Either (a) wire `setPhaseCompletion` (currently commented on lines 149-161) to track per-task completion and gate the "Next Task" button until the current task reports `onCompleteChange(true)`; or (b) accept that completion gating is intentionally disabled (the upstream Reading Advantage may have removed gating to reduce friction for younger students) and delete the dead `onCompleteChange` prop from `TaskIntroduction` to remove the misleading interface. Either way, the no-op `() => {}` on line 387 should be replaced with the real handler or the prop should be removed. Track under a `primary_advantage_lesson_phase_gating_<date>` track.

title: Dead `useRef`s `currentTaskRef` and `isTransitioningRef` declared and updated in effects, but never read anywhere in the file
evidence: Lines 65-67 declare `const currentTaskRef = useRef(currentTask);` and `const isTransitioningRef = useRef(isTransitioning);` with the comment "Use refs to access current values in useEffect without causing re-runs" (line 65). Lines 70-76 contain two effects that simply write to these refs: `currentTaskRef.current = currentTask;` and `isTransitioningRef.current = isTransitioning;`. `grep -n "currentTaskRef\|isTransitioningRef" lesson-progress-bar.tsx` returns only lines 66, 67, 71, 75 — no `.current` reads anywhere. The refs are write-only.
impact: Low. Each write-only `useRef` allocates a stable object that never changes; the only cost is two unused refs and two unnecessary effect runs per state change. The comment on line 65 suggests an earlier version of the code read these refs inside a `setTimeout` or async callback, but the call sites were removed (probably during the cleanup that also commented out lines 149-188 and 250-255). The dead code is also a maintenance hazard: future contributors may add a `.current` read assuming the ref is intentional.

The state values `currentTask` and `isTransitioning` are already in scope wherever the effects would need them, and any closure-captured value can be read directly from the state instead of via a ref. If a ref is genuinely needed in the future (e.g., inside an async function that may run after the closure has been garbage-collected), add it at the call site rather than preemptively at the top of the component. Track under a `primary_advantage_dead_ref_cleanup_<date>` chore.

title: Dead `useCallback` import and dead `skipTask` helper; both are referenced in commented-out code but never reachable from the live component
evidence: Line 7 imports `useCallback` from React. The only reference to `useCallback` is inside a commented-out block on lines 149-161 (`// const updatePhaseCompletion = useCallback(`). No live code uses `useCallback`. The `skipTask` helper is declared on lines 491-526 with `const skipTask = async (Task: number) => { ... };` — `grep -n "skipTask" lesson-progress-bar.tsx` returns only the declaration on line 491; no JSX or handler ever invokes it. The body of `skipTask` is entirely commented out (lines 492-525), and the only live statement is `setCurrentTask(Task + 1)` on line 512.
impact: Low. The dead `useCallback` import (line 7) is removed at build time by tree-shaking but adds bundle metadata; the dead `skipTask` function is tree-shaken if unused, but if any future contributor reads `Task` as `task` (a common naming convention), the function may silently misbehave. More importantly, the absence of an invoke site means no UI ever offers a "Skip Task" button — the lesson is linear and cannot be skipped, which is a feature gap rather than a bug. The previously-shipped version of this component likely had a skip button that was removed during the cleanup.
recommendation: Delete lines 491-526 (the `skipTask` function). Either delete the `useCallback` import on line 7 (preferred — no other consumer in the file) or keep it if a future refactor reintroduces the `updatePhaseCompletion` callback. If "skip task" is a desired feature, reintroduce the button with a proper `onClick` handler that wires through `setPhaseCompletion` and `updateUserLessonProgress` — see finding 003 for the broader phase-gating context. Track under a `primary_advantage_dead_skip_task_cleanup_<date>` chore.

title: `animate-shake` class referenced on Next button but no `@keyframes shake` or Tailwind config defining the class exists in this app
evidence: Line 78 declares `const [shakeButton, setShakeButton] = useState(false);`. Line 648 reads `className={`... ${shakeButton ? "animate-shake" : ""}`}`. `grep -n "animate-shake\|@keyframes shake" apps/primary-advantage/` finds only the usage on line 648 — no `@keyframes shake` definition in `apps/primary-advantage/styles/globals.css` (only `animate-glow` on line 147 is defined) and no `tailwind.config.{js,ts}` extending the animation. The setter `setShakeButton` is only called inside a commented-out block on line 252. Therefore `shakeButton` is always `false` and the class `animate-shake` is never applied at runtime. Even if it were applied, Tailwind v4 would not generate the utility because the keyframes are not defined.
impact: Low. The dead state and the missing keyframe definition both reflect a half-finished UX feature: the developer planned a "shake the Next button when the user tries to advance without completing the current task" affordance, but the gating logic and the animation were both removed. The current behavior is correct (the Next button advances whenever clicked), so there is no functional regression, only dead code and a misleading string in the className.
recommendation: Delete line 78 (`shakeButton` state). Optionally delete lines 251-255 (the commented-out gating block) and remove the `${shakeButton ? "animate-shake" : ""}` fragment on line 648. If a future UX wants to shake the button on invalid clicks, add a real `@keyframes shake` in `apps/primary-advantage/styles/globals.css`, a corresponding Tailwind v4 `@theme` or `@utility` entry, and a real setter call site. Track under a `primary_advantage_shake_button_cleanup_<date>` chore.

title: Initial-load effect closes over `fetchCurrentPhase` from outside the effect; ESLint `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` would flag this and the body is recreated every render
evidence: Lines 82-147 declare the initial-load effect. Inside the effect body (lines 86-134) is a nested `fetchCurrentPhase` async function. The effect itself calls `fetchCurrentPhase()` on line 139 inside a `setTimeout`. The dependency array on line 147 is `[initialLoadComplete, assignment?.id, setTimer, setPaused]`. Two issues: (1) `fetchCurrentPhase` is defined inside the effect, so it doesn't need to be in the deps (the linter accepts this); (2) `setTimer` and `setPaused` come from `useContext(QuizContext)` on line 63 — per the React docs, `useState` setters are stable references but `useContext` may return new function references if the provider re-creates them. Per `apps/primary-advantage/contexts/question-context.tsx:38`, the provider returns `{ timer, setPaused, setTimer }` from `useState` hooks, which are stable. So the deps are technically correct, but the `setTimeout(() => fetchCurrentPhase(), 100)` on line 138-140 introduces an extra 100ms delay that is not justified — the fetch could fire immediately on mount.
impact: Low. The 100ms `setTimeout` is a deliberate "quick initial load" comment (line 140) but functionally it just delays the first paint of the lesson by 100ms. For a primary-student app where the lesson UI is the primary surface, an extra 100ms before the lesson phase content renders is a perceptible but minor regression. The `timeoutId = setTimeout(...)` declaration on line 138 is captured by the `clearTimeout(timeoutId)` cleanup on line 145, which is correct.
recommendation: Drop the `setTimeout` and call `fetchCurrentPhase()` synchronously on line 139 (the effect body still runs in a microtask after mount). Or, if the 100ms delay is intentional to avoid layout thrash from the loading spinner, document the reason in a comment. Track under a `primary_advantage_initial_load_delay_<date>` chore.

title: `nextTask` advances to `newTask = Task + 1` but writes the *post-advance* progress; a server-side failure leaves the local state ahead of the server
evidence: Line 265 reads `const newTask = Task + 1;` (the task the user is *moving to*). Line 310 writes `progress: Math.round((newTask / 14) * 100)`. If the fetch fails (line 321 `else` branch), the function logs the error (line 322-326), resets the fade/loading flags (line 327-329), and falls through. Critically, the local state has *not* been advanced: `setCurrentTask(newTask)` is only called inside the `response.ok` branch on line 316. So on failure the user sees the same phase they were on. But on success, the local state and the server progress are aligned. The bug: the `await saveArticleToFlashcard(assignment?.articleId as string)` call on line 277 (for `newTask === 7`, the multiple-choice phase, after vocabulary flashcards) is awaited inline before the progress fetch. If `saveArticleToFlashcard` throws or hangs, the user is stuck on the transition (the spinner on lines 589, 624, 657 keeps spinning because `setIsTransitioning(false)` is in the `finally` block on line 339, but `setPhaseLoading(false)` is inside the `response.ok`/`else` branches and would not be called if `saveArticleToFlashcard` threw before line 305). Reading the `try/catch` on line 262-336: a throw inside the `await saveArticleToFlashcard` would be caught by the `catch` block on line 331 and `setPhaseLoading(false)` would fire on line 336, so the UI does recover.
impact: Medium. The "save flashcard then advance" coupling is fragile: if the user is on task 6 (sentence collection) and clicks Next, the code sets `newTask = 7`, calls `saveArticleToFlashcard`, and only then POSTs to `/api/assignments/{id}` to mark task 7 reached. The save happens before the progress update, which is the correct ordering (don't mark the lesson advanced until the flashcard is saved), but the two calls are not transactional — if the flashcard save succeeds and the progress POST fails, the server has flashcard data without a matching progress entry. For a primary-student app the flashcard is a study artifact and the progress is the lesson ledger; the mismatch is recoverable on the next reload (`saveArticleToFlashcard` is idempotent, but the server does not deduplicate).
recommendation: Wrap the two side effects in a single server action or a server-side transaction. Specifically, move `saveArticleToFlashcard` into the assignment progress controller (`assignmentController.ts:319-350`) so the save and the progress update share a transaction; or move both into a server action `actions/assignment.ts:completeLessonTask(assignmentId, articleId, newTask, timeSpent)` that the client calls atomically. Track under a `primary_advantage_lesson_progress_transaction_<date>` track that also audits other places where the client chains two server calls.

title: `previousTask` does not POST to the server; navigating back is a local-only state change with no server-side revert
evidence: Lines 347-378 implement `previousTask`. The function sets `isTransitioning`, computes `newPhase = currentTask - 1`, animates fade out/in, and finally sets `currentTask(newPhase)` on line 365 — but never POSTs to `/api/assignments/{id}` to revert the server-side progress. Compare with `nextTask` (lines 305-313) which always POSTs. The result: the server thinks the user is on task N (or N+1) while the client shows task N-1. On reload, the initial-load effect on lines 82-147 fetches the server's stored progress and computes `taskNumber = ceil(progress / taskWidth)`, which snaps the user forward to where the server thinks they are — discarding the back-navigation.
impact: Medium. The "Previous Task" button (lines 617) is a UX illusion: the user clicks it, the UI animates back, the next page render shows the previous phase, but any reload (browser refresh, navigation, switching tabs and coming back) restores the forward position. For a primary-student app where the previous-task affordance is used to re-read the introduction or review vocabulary, this is a misleading feature. The Reading Advantage upstream likely wired `previousTask` to a server-side `decrementProgress` endpoint; the fork appears to have removed that endpoint or never ported it.
recommendation: Either (a) add a `POST /api/assignments/{id}` body parameter `direction: "back"` (or a new endpoint `POST /api/assignments/{id}/regress`) and call it from `previousTask` on line 365, or (b) remove the "Previous Task" button on lines 612-642 and the `previousTask` helper if backward navigation is intentionally unsupported. Track under a `primary_advantage_back_navigation_server_sync_<date>` track that also audits other client-only state changes that diverge from the server.

title: `skipTask` would let the user advance without server validation if its body were ever uncommented
evidence: `skipTask` on lines 491-526 has its body entirely commented out (lines 492-525); the only live statement is `setCurrentTask(Task + 1)` on line 512. If the comments are ever uncommented (or if a future contributor refactors and the `setCurrentTask` line is moved into an `async` block), the function will advance the user to the next task on the client without any server-side call. The function name "skip" suggests this is intentional (skips persistence), but the lack of any UI binding to `skipTask` means the dead code is a footgun: a future maintainer who wires a Skip button will skip the server entirely.
impact: Medium. This is a latent bug: today, no UI invokes `skipTask`, so the bug does not fire. But the function exists, is exported from the component closure, and is reachable from any future JSX. A primary-student app that silently skips server-side progress would desynchronize the user's lesson ledger from their actual journey.
recommendation: Delete `skipTask` entirely (see finding 005) or, if a skip feature is desired, replace the body with `setCurrentTask(Task + 1); await fetch("/api/assignments/{id}", { method: "POST", body: JSON.stringify({ articleId: assignment?.articleId, progress: Math.round(((Task + 1) / 14) * 100), timeSpent: timer, skipped: true }) });` — i.e., the server must learn about the skip. Track under a `primary_advantage_skip_task_server_sync_<date>` track.

title: Mobile accordion `maxHeight` effect depends only on `isExpanded`; if the inner task list height changes after expand, the accordion stays at the old (truncated) height
evidence: Lines 528-532 implement `useEffect(() => { if (contentRef.current) { setMaxHeight(isExpanded ? `${contentRef.current.scrollHeight}px` : "0px"); } }, [isExpanded]);`. The effect only re-runs when `isExpanded` changes. But the inner content (lines 747-778 — the task list) does not change height during a single expand/collapse cycle: it iterates `Array.from({ length: 14 }, ...)` which is a fixed size, and each row's height is determined by the rendered task name (`getTaskDisplayName(index + 1)`), which is a translation key with a static fallback. So in practice the content height is constant. The effect works correctly today. However, if a future feature adds dynamic content (e.g., a "current task indicator" with an animated chevron, or a per-task XP badge), the height will change after expand but the effect will not re-fire, so the accordion will clip the new content.
impact: Low. Today this is correct because the task list is fixed-size. The bug is latent and will fire as soon as the sidebar grows dynamic content. The mobile accordion is the only place in the file where the height depends on rendered content.
recommendation: Either (a) add a `ResizeObserver` on `contentRef.current` that calls `setMaxHeight(`${contentRef.current.scrollHeight}px`)` whenever the content resizes, gated by `isExpanded`; or (b) replace the CSS `maxHeight` transition with `max-height: none; height: auto` and rely on the browser's content-size-driven layout (no transition, but no clipping risk). The current pattern is the "JS-driven CSS transition" idiom that breaks for dynamic content. Track under a `primary_advantage_accordion_dynamic_content_<date>` chore.

title: `QuizContext` starts a `setInterval` that ticks `timer` on mount and runs unconditionally; the lesson-progress bar starts the timer before the user clicks "Start Lesson"
evidence: Line 63 reads `const { timer, setPaused, setTimer } = useContext(QuizContext);`. Per `apps/primary-advantage/contexts/question-context.tsx:23-41`, `QuizContextProvider` runs `useEffect` on line 27 that starts a `setInterval` ticking `timer` every 1s unless `paused`. The interval starts on mount of the provider (which is mounted in `lesson-card.tsx` per finding LR-primary-advantage-038-007's sibling context). `setPaused(true)` is the only way to stop it. The lesson-progress bar:
impact: Medium. The "lesson time spent" metric is inflated by the time between mount and the user clicking "Start Lesson". For a primary-student app where the timer is part of the motivation loop ("you read this in 5 minutes!"), the recorded time is artificially high. The server persists `timeSpent` on every `nextTask` call (line 311), so the inflated value is committed to the database. On reload, the inflated `timeSpent` is restored (line 109) and the countdown continues from the wrong baseline. The Reading Advantage upstream may have intentionally started the timer on mount; the fork should confirm whether this is the desired behavior.
recommendation: Either (a) start the timer paused and call `setPaused(false)` only inside `startLesson` on success (around line 219), or (b) zero the timer on `startLesson` (call `setTimer(0)` before line 195) and start the interval at the same moment. The current behavior mixes "mount time" with "lesson time" and the user has no signal for when the timer actually started. Track under a `primary_advantage_lesson_timer_lifecycle_<date>` track alongside the broader QuizContext provider audit (this affects every consumer of `QuizContext`, not just `lesson-progress-bar`).

title: `lesson-task-mcq.tsx` references undefined `update` and `session` variables (ReferenceError)
evidence: Line 50 destructures `const { user } = useSession();`. The hook `useSession()` from `@reading-advantage/auth-client` returns `{ user, isAuthenticated, isLoading }` (confirmed at `packages/auth-client/src/index.ts:16-23`). It does NOT return `session` or `update`. Lines 208-210 call `update({ user: { ...session?.user } })`, referencing two identifiers that are not in scope. Both `update` and `session` will be `ReferenceError` at runtime. This same broken pattern appears across at least 10 other lesson components (lesson-sentence-cloze-test, lesson-sentence-flashcard, lesson-vocabulary-flashcard-card, lesson-sentence-matching, lesson-sentence-order-word, lesson-sentence-order, lesson-vocabulary-matching, task-lesson-summary, and this file's sibling lesson-task-saq.tsx), indicating a systematic migration artifact: the code was written for NextAuth.js's `useSession()` (which returns `{ data: { user, session }, update }`) and was never adapted to the shared auth-client's `useSession()` API.
impact: The `handleFinishQuiz` callback on line 193-217 calls this code path. When a student completes the MCQ quiz and clicks "Finish Quiz", the `startTransition` callback fires `update(...)` on line 208. This will throw a `ReferenceError`, preventing `state` from being set to `QuestionState.COMPLETED` on line 207. The UI will remain stuck in the in-progress state, and the score will never be persisted or displayed. This is a fork-specific regression because the shared auth-client replaced NextAuth.js but these components were not updated to match the new hook API.
recommendation: Replace the broken `update({ user: { ...session?.user } })` call with either `updateUserSession()` from the auth-client's actions, or remove it entirely since `finishQuiz` already persists the score server-side. The client-side session cache update is redundant for quiz completion. If a cache update is truly needed, use `useAuth()` from `@reading-advantage/auth-client` which returns the full `AuthContextValue` including auth actions.

title: `lesson-task-mcq.tsx` contains large commented-out dead code blocks
evidence: Lines 33-37 contain a commented-out results/progress/total/state/summary object. Lines 85-121 contain a fully commented-out `fetchQuizData` effect function (37 lines) that was replaced by the client-side `useEffect` on lines 52-61 that pulls questions from `article.multipleChoiceQuestions`. The `fetchQuizData` code would have fetched from `/api/articles/questions/${articleId}?questionType=...`, which is the older API-driven approach.
impact: Dead code increases cognitive load during maintenance. The commented-out path also documents a design alternative (server-fetched vs. props-driven quiz) that may confuse future developers. No runtime impact.
recommendation: Remove the commented-out blocks. If the API-driven approach is ever needed again, it belongs in source control history.

title: `lesson-task-mcq.tsx` uses `as any` type escapes on state variables
evidence: Line 47 declares `const [activeQuestion, setActiveQuestion] = useState(null) as any;` and line 48 declares `const [responses, setResponses] = useState<any[]>([]);`. Both defeat TypeScript type checking. The `responses` array is later populated with objects having `{ question, answer, isCorrect }` shape (lines 126-130) but no interface or type guard enforces this shape. The `activeQuestion` state is typed as `any` and compared against option strings on lines 449-456.
impact: Any code modification that changes the shape of response objects or options will not be caught by the type checker. Low severity because the code is functionally correct within the current component boundary.
recommendation: Define `interface QuizResponse { question: string; answer: string; isCorrect: string; }` and type `responses` as `QuizResponse[]`. Type `activeQuestion` as `string | null` instead of `null as any`.
